content: Occupational exposure to carbon monoxide (CO) at the three workplaces under investigation has been associated with an increased number of deaths due to heart disease. Detailed information is required regarding the daily exposure levels of workers, who engage in varying degrees of physical activity, to specific sources of CO within their work environments. This data should also be correlated with the workers' smoking habits and their non-occupational exposure to CO. Regardless of the source of CO, the rate at which CO is eliminated from the blood depends on the concentration of CO in the surrounding air. For smokers with elevated levels of carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) who are also exposed to CO in their workplace, the excretion of CO from their bodies is proportionally delayed. Since the recommended occupational exposure standard for CO is designed to protect employees with coronary heart disease (CHD), it is essential to assess the prevalence of this condition among the general workforce. Friedberg has defined CHD as clinical heart disease caused by lesions in the coronary arteries. However, the term CHD is more commonly used to describe the process of atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries, which leads to disturbances in the myocardial blood supply. It is in this latter context that the term is applied in the criteria document. A study of autopsies in a stabilized population of 30,000 individuals revealed that CHD was the cause of death in 40% of the males. Friedberg has stated that the diagnosis of coronary (atherosclerotic) heart disease refers to its clinical manifestations and not merely the presence of atherosclerotic lesions. Extensive pathological lesions may exist but cannot be diagnosed unless they produce overt clinical symptoms or are detected through coronary angiography. In most cases, the first clinical manifestation of CHD is either angina pectoris or a myocardial infarction. According to the Framingham study conducted in Massachusetts by the U.S. Public Health Service, CHD first manifested as sudden death in one-sixth of the cases. Metabolic evidence of myocardial hypoxia has been observed in patients with coronary artery disease during acute exposure to CO concentrations sufficient to produce a COHb content of less than 9%. This finding highlights that in patients with coronary artery disease, coronary blood flow does not increase at this level of COHb saturation, unlike in control subjects. This underscores the potential consequences for individuals with CHD who have COHb levels below 9%. It is important to emphasize that these coronary patients were at rest and not subjected to physical exertion. The additional stress of exercise, as documented earlier in the study by Knelsen, further supports the conclusion that workers with CHD, particularly those who smoke, should not be exposed to CO concentrations that result in COHb levels exceeding 5%. Similarly, the effects of CO on behavior remain inconsistent, with several mechanisms proposed to explain the differing results.
